extracted.intended_audience: new comedians and comedy writers learning joke structure
extracted.subtask_description: A how-to for writing stand-up 'Broken Assumption' jokes: teach the setup → audience assumption → punchline flip structure, concrete exercises, and types of shifts (who/what/where/when/why/how). Geared toward beginners building core joke-writing skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken Assumption joke structure
rubrics_metrics.description: setup → audience makes an assumption → punchline flips it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure is crystal clear: setup → audience makes an assumption → punchline flips it. No complicated formulas—just a straight path to the punchline. Examples: Jim Gaffigan, John Mulaney, Bill Engvall quotes illustrate the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot assumptions in the setup
rubrics_metrics.description: First, figure out what is being implied by the setup — what the audience is assuming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the implicit information (who/what/where/when/why/how) the listener is filling in. The article emphasizes parsing explicit vs. implicit info to locate which assumption you can break.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a new meaning (use But Statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a new meaning (often the opposite of the assumption) using a 'But Statement' to juxtapose normal vs. inappropriate interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But Statement form: '(Thing that implies normal assumption), BUT (something that breaks the assumption)'. Example: 'The menu said “chef’s special,” BUT they really meant ___.' Use the blank to playfully fill in the broken assumption and let your comedic voice come through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imply the new meaning with the punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a punchline that implies the new meaning rather than over-explaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Last, write a punchline that implies the new meaning (e.g., 'Turns out “chef’s special” means “whatever expires at midnight.”' or 'It’s so special the health inspector took pictures.'). Keep the implication light and playfully inappropriate when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Break identity assumptions about 'who' until the punchline reveals a different person or role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bill Engvall's golf story flips from 'another golfer' to 'a driver on the highway.' Labelled as a 'Who-Shift.' Use to reveal an unexpected identity or role for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: What-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift the assumed object or event into something else unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Stephen Wright's 'Cross-country skiing is great if you live in a small country.' Use the punchline to change what the audience thinks the premise refers to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the assumed location to an unexpected place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Stephen Wright: 'I installed a skylight in my house. The people who live above me are furious.' The assumed locations are reversed or reinterpreted for the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: When-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Break assumptions about timing or the temporal context of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bill Engvall's skiing line uses an implied timing shift. Note: timing is often left vague — 'The other day' — to avoid locking the joke into unnecessary specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the assumed reason or motivation behind an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steve Martin's 'place a woman on a pedestal – high enough so you can look up her dress.' The punchline reframes the motivation and exposes a darker/inappropriate intent for comedic surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: How-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift assumptions about the manner in which something happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steve Martin: 'I gave my cat a bath... The fur would stick to my tongue' — flips from 'put cat in bath' to 'licked the cat.' Use 'how' shifts to surprise by changing the action's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit information; don't give the audience too much
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit unnecessary details (especially 'when') so the audience focuses on the assumptions that matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When is often left out because it usually doesn't play a role; use short phrases ('The other day') if needed. If you give too much info, the audience must sort through extraneous details and may miss the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety from the initial interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first, safe interpretation to set up a secure frame before breaking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'safety' of the joke comes from the first interpretation; the punchline's shift breaks that assumption. Establish a believable, ordinary setup so the flip lands as surprise rather than confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific prompts and constraints (practice method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tight prompts and short timed exercises to produce many punchlines quickly; don't overthink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actionable practice: 'set a timer for 2 minutes and write. Do not overthink.' Use provided prompts (restaurant menu, wedding invitation, spouse/teacher/boss setups) and return to the mechanics (spot assumption → But Statement → punchline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor non-sexual or unexpectedly mundane solutions for sexual setups
rubrics_metrics.description: When a setup implies sexual content, the less sexual your solution, the funnier it will often be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint example: For 'My spouse said we need more excitement in the bedroom,' a fog machine or lasers (non-sexual) are funnier than obvious sexual responses. Use incongruity between expectation and actual solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and progression to advanced joke types
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken Assumption jokes are adaptable to many topics and build skills for more complex joke types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you master surprise via broken assumptions, you can more easily write exaggerations, contradictions, misdirection, long-form stories, rule-of-three lists, puns, callbacks, self-deprecation, etc. Use broken-assumption practice as foundational training.
